column1: # Conformance corpus index -- consumed by scripts/conformance_kit.sh.
# Format: <language><TAB><path>, one row per fixture. Multiple rows per
# language are allowed and are measured together.
# Paths are resolved RELATIVE TO THIS FILE'S DIRECTORY, never to $PWD, so an
# out-of-tree language module can ship its own corpus.tsv next to its fixtures
# (RFC "Language module anatomy": languages/<lang>/conformance/) and the kit
# The language column is EXPLICIT rather than derived from the file extension.
# Two reasons: the `duckdb` adapter has no file extensions at all
# (ast_supported_languages() reports an empty list for it), and `sample.sql`
# is a legitimate fixture for both `sql` (tree-sitter) and `duckdb` (native).
# Languages here are intersected with ast_supported_languages() at run time, so
# a row for a language this build compiled out is skipped, and a language the
# build registers but this file omits is reported VOID (no fixture) -- never
# Most fixtures are existing committed test data rather than new files: a
# fixture already exercised by another suite is one that is already known to
# parse, which keeps a harness artifact from being reported as a conformance
# WHY SO MANY FIXTURES PER LANGUAGE. The ../unparse_leaf_text/sample.* set
# covers 26 of the 27 registered languages in one place, which makes it the
# natural spine of this corpus -- but those files were written to exercise LEAF
# TEXT, so several of them have only a no-argument function (`void main()`,
# `auto greet() -> std::string`). A corpus like that cannot distinguish "this
# module does not extract parameters" from "nothing in the corpus has a
# parameter to extract", and the first revision of this corpus duly reported
# cpp and dart as non-conformant when the fixtures were the problem. So every
# language that has richer committed test data gets it listed here as well.
# The checks still carry their own source-side guards; this is belt and braces,
# because a fixture gap reported as a defect is worse than no check at all.
